newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FORECAST - Telecom's Q3 profit seen as flat.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Telecom's Q3 profit seen as flat.

text.p: Concerns about Telecom New Zealand's profits have seen its share price savaged in recent weeks, but analysts on Thursday said the market was being short sighted.

True, Telecom is expected to post a flat third quarter profit when it reports on Tuesday -- something close to last year's NZ$182.2 million. But that includes what are likely to be substantial losses sustained by Australian subsidiary Pacific Star, which Telecom is in the process of selling.
"Basically Telecom's got one problem child, which is quite large, but it's not part of the core business and it's not going to be there for ever," said Kevin Bennett, analyst at Doyle Paterson Brown.
No one is really sure how large the Pacific Star's loss contribution will be this quarter, but analysts suggest it may be somewhere between $11-$20 million.
"I think Pac Star has the potential to obscure the operating result. People should really, when they start looking at these numbers, be factoring it out," Bennett said.
In the last three weeks, Telecom's share price has fallen from a high of NZ$7.58 to a low of $6.90 as brokers downgraded earnings forecasts.
In addition to the expected Pacific Star losses, the slowing New Zealand economy and growing competition have been cited as negatives for the stock.
Analysts said BellSouth had become increasingly competitive in the last two or three quarters, and there would be interest in what that was doing to Telecom's cellular prices and volumes.
But it was unreasonable to assume that a company of Telecom's size could be totally insulated to an economy that has slowed as much as New Zealand's has.

"We don't think there's any reason to cry wolf. The simple fact of life is that if the economy is only growing half or a third as fast as it was a year ago, it's a lot harder to grow your business," Bennett said.
"I mean, we're not talking about the company going back to growth rates similar to the economy."
Guy Hallwright at First NZ Capital said the slowing economy and falling prices in a competitive environment were naturally affecting Telecom's profit, offsetting to a certain extent revenue growth.

"But they certainly wouldn't be producing anything like the flatish results that we're now seeing. You've got to bear in mind that it is to a very large extent one-off factors that are depressing profits at the moment," he said.
Growth in the cellular phone market was on the up again, enhanced services were growing strongly, and there were no immediate concerns about national and international call volumes, he said.
One area of concern for the future was the development of Internet technologies.
Analysts said the ability to place telephone calls through the Internet would become an area of intense competition and had the potential to cannibalise Telecom's core business.
"If people use the Internet, they won't be using the standard telephony systems," said Cavill White analyst Sarndra Urlich.
"I don't think that's something to worry about immediately, but it will come in in the next couple of years and it's all stuff to think about," she said.
Analysts have pegged back their forecasts of Telecom's full year profit result to around $740 million from $770-80 million.
"But in aggregate, we think Telecommunications is still and will continue to be a growth industry," Bennett said.
Ameritech and Bell Atlantic together own 49.9 percent of Telecom, which will report its third quarter profit result at 9.30 a.m. (2030 GMT) on Tuesday.
